docs.title: Uber Career Prep Open Source Playbook
docs.text: This strategy and execution playbook outlines the necessary steps required to create a Career Prep program similar to Uber's. It outlines the steps, recommendations, and guidance for building a program that helps undergraduate engineering students enter the tech industry.

docs.title: What's in this playbook?
docs.text:
• :material-list-status: Planning Your Program

    A step-by-step guide through all 17 planning stages — from reviewing program resources to building your alumni network.

  • :material-account-group: Roles & Responsibilities

    Detailed breakdowns of every Core Program Team role and volunteer position, including time commitments and responsibilities.

  • :material-rocket-launch: Program Execution

    A three-phase execution framework covering fellow selection, workshops, and internship outcomes.

  • :material-folder-open: Resources

    Open-source templates, task lists, checklists, trackers, and role descriptions — everything you need to get started.

docs.title: About Uber Career Prep
docs.text:
Uber Career Prep (UCP) is an unpaid, virtual fellowship program for undergraduate engineering students. It aims to provide transparency and guidance for starting a STEM career in tech, focusing on removing barriers and supporting students' right to learn and succeed.

At a glance:

  • 5 virtual workshops led by Uber staff, scheduled every 7 weeks over ~8 months
  • 40 hours of instruction total
  • 1:1 mentorship with an Uber software engineer
  • 4 mock interviews and 5 technical practice assignments
  • Invitation to interview for a paid internship at the end of the cohort

A key driver of this program's success is that it's run by the Engineering Team — for future engineers.

docs.title: Program Execution Overview
docs.text:
The program is executed in three distinct phases:

Phase 1          Phase 2              Phase 3
─────────────    ───────────────────  ──────────────────────────
Selection of  →  Workshops        →   Post-Workshop
Fellows          (Core Learning)      (Internship Interviews
                                       + Outcomes)
Phase Focus Key Output Phase 1 — Selection Application, review, and cohort interviews Confirmed cohort of fellows Phase 2 — Workshops 5 workshop sessions over ~8 months Fellows complete 40 hrs of instruction Phase 3 — Outcomes Internship interviews, offers, retrospective Placed interns + program learnings

docs.title: Phase 1 — Selection of Fellows
docs.text:
This phase covers the application process, marketing, and cohort interviews that result in a confirmed group of program fellows.

Key Requirements:

  • Finalize cohort logistics before the application launches.
  • Marketing efforts should reach the target audience.
  • Application review process should be thorough and unbiased.
  • Cohort interviews should be conducted efficiently and fairly.

docs.title: Cohort Planning
docs.text:
Action

Confirm program logistics before the application launches.

Guidance
  • Follow the Step by Step Planning Overview and the Execution Checklist for Cohort Planning.
  • Ensure alignment with the program timeline.
Considerations
  • Is there enough time to finalize logistics before the cohort launches?

docs.title: Marketing the Program & Application
docs.text:
Action

The Core Program and Recruiting Teams collaborate on developing and implementing the application's marketing strategy.

Guidance
  • Link all marketing materials back to one main application.
  • Marketing materials should have virtual and digital options.
  • Marketing materials should include one contact point.
  • Marketing materials should have a clear call to action.
Considerations
  • What is the desired duration of the application period?
  • What timeframe is allocated for marketing the application?
  • Which organizations are targeted for partnerships?
  • What channels will be employed to promote the applications?
  • Are the marketing assets compatible across all intended platforms?
  • Where do you want to market the program?
  • Which schools or geographic locations will you market the program to? For example, if you want to reach students with different levels of access to opportunities, consider focusing on affordable colleges like state colleges.

docs.title: Application Review
docs.text:
Action

Establish an application review procedure.

Guidance
  • Ensure the application process is approved by the Legal Team.
  • Establish clear application review guidelines.
  • Involve multiple reviewers to reduce bias.
  • List target schools/organizations for reviewers.
  • Use "knockout" questions for easy filtering.
  • Allocate sufficient time for application review.
  • Agree on the maximum number of interviewees.
  • Determine review time per application.
  • Require reviewers to justify recommendations.
  • Minimize application questions.
  • Maintain consistent question types.
  • Use filterable question types.
  • Clearly communicate the application process and timeline to candidates.
Considerations
  • What applicant tracking platform is used by your company?
  • Can you use the same platform for educational opportunities?
  • What's the number of projected applications and how will the review schedule be divided?
  • Are there specific recruiting targets or metrics that will impact the application review process?
  • Which critical questions will help obtain vital candidate information?

Phase 2 — Workshops :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Phase 2 — Workshops: Core Program Learning Sessions
docs.text:
This phase covers the preparation and execution of all workshop sessions across the cohort.

Key Requirements:

  • Curriculum delivery should be engaging and well-paced.
  • Balance lecture-style sessions with interactive activities and breakout groups.
  • Workshops should not conflict with students' exam schedules.

docs.title: Workshop Preparation
docs.text:
Action

Prepare to host workshops using the Workshop Execution Checklist.

Guidance
  • Ensure the agenda is created with ~4 weeks lead-time to recruit and train volunteers as needed.
  • Schedule mock interviews at least one week in advance to confirm interviewer availability and set time aside for rescheduling.
  • Host a dry run with the MC to address all workshop one-off requirements.
  • Schedule dry runs with speakers as needed.

docs.title: Workshop Execution
docs.text:
Action

Host workshops according to the program timeline.

Guidance
  • Conduct weekly Core Program Team meetings to discuss issues and questions.
  • Maintain program flexibility; promptly incorporate feedback for participant benefit.
  • Schedule breaks.
  • Design engaging agendas with diverse formats (e.g., panel discussions vs. single speakers).
  • Workshops will not be recorded to promote live participation.
Considerations
  • What is the degree of participant involvement in the workshops?
  • Does participant attention stay consistent, or are there drop-offs in engagement at certain times?
  • At what points are participants most likely to turn their cameras on or off?
  • How will your team address live engagement vs. AI bots and note-taking?

:material-arrow-left: Phase 1 Phase 3 :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Phase 3 — Post-Workshop: Internship Interviews & Outcomes
docs.text:
This phase covers the final interview stage, offer process, and program wrap-up.

Key Requirements:

  • Internship interviews should be conducted in a manner that mimics actual interviews.
  • Offer process should be managed efficiently and professionally.
  • Follow-up and relocation planning should be addressed.

docs.title: Internship Interviews and Outcomes
docs.text:
Action

The Core Program Team and the Recruiting Team will collaborate to guide students through the final interview stage.

Guidance
  • Ensure a streamlined process to advance students efficiently through interview stages that aligns with your company's recruiting process.
  • Communicate a clear timeline to students regarding offer or rejection decisions.
  • Collaborate with the Recruiting Team to determine if program engagement and metrics will factor into offer evaluations.
  • Promptly monitor and record program outcomes, including:
    • Updating program trackers with final results
    • Informing relevant stakeholders
    • Acknowledging and thanking volunteers
  • Provide concluding remarks with encouragement for all cohort members, regardless of offer status.
Considerations
  • How will the metrics be communicated to key stakeholders?
  • What effect will this cohort's metrics have on subsequent cohorts?
  • What key takeaways were identified from the experience?

:material-arrow-left: Phase 2 Resources :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Mission
docs.text: To provide undergraduate engineering students who have potential — but may not have equal access to opportunities — with the skills that will help them gain entrance to the tech industry and beyond.

docs.title: Why This Matters
docs.text:
Many talented students enter college with the drive and aptitude to succeed in a tech career, but face barriers that their peers with more access do not:

  • Fewer industry connections and mentors
  • Less exposure to internship recruiting processes
  • Limited practice with technical interviews
  • Uncertainty about how to present themselves professionally

UCP directly addresses these gaps through structured mentorship, practice, and transparency.

docs.title: Alumni as a Force Multiplier
docs.text: After each cohort, cultivate a strong alumni network and integrate them into as many volunteer positions as possible. Alumni are already familiar with the program and offer invaluable technical guidance, best practices, and relevant advice — significantly aiding current cohort members in overcoming challenges like imposter syndrome.

docs.title: What is the Career Prep Program?
docs.text:
Uber Career Prep (UCP) is an unpaid, virtual fellowship program for undergraduate engineering students. It aims to provide transparency and guidance for starting a STEM career in tech.

The program focuses on removing barriers and supporting students' right to learn and succeed — because Uber believes everyone has potential, but not everyone has equal access to opportunity.

docs.title: Program Structure
docs.text:
Fellows attend 5 virtual workshops led by Uber staff, scheduled every 7 weeks over approximately 8 months, completing 40 hours of instruction in total.

Throughout the cohort, each fellow receives:

  • 1:1 mentorship from an Uber software engineer
  • 4 mock interviews with structured feedback
  • 5 technical practice assignments that build on each other in difficulty

docs.title: Workshop Topics
docs.text:
Workshops cover both technical and career-advancing subjects, including:

  • Technical Mock Interviews
  • 1:1 Mentorship
  • Clear Code and Communication
  • Negotiations
  • Technical Competencies and Problem Solving
  • LinkedIn and Resume Best Practices

docs.title: Internship Pipeline
docs.text:
At the end of the cohort, fellows who meet all program requirements are invited to interview for a paid internship role starting at the next internship cycle.

Key success factor

A key element and driver of success of this program is that it's run by the Engineering Team for future engineers.

docs.title: Planning Your Program
docs.text:
This section breaks down the program's key components and provides step-by-step guidance on how to execute a successful Career Prep program.

Each step includes:

  • Action — what you need to do
  • Guidance — how to approach it
  • Considerations — questions to ask yourself before moving on

docs.title: The 17 Steps at a Glance
docs.text:
Step Topic 1 Review Program Resources and Create Program Templates 2 Engage your Leadership Team 3 Create Program Timeline and Set Key Milestones 4 Confirm Core Program Team 5 Confirm if your Program is Virtual or In-Person 6 Confirm Length of the Program 7 Confirm Size of your Cohort 8 Confirm the Dates/Times of your Workshops 9 Confirm Program Budget 10 Align Recruiting Strategy & Confirm Eligibility Requirements 11 Create your Program Curriculum 12 Create Volunteer Plan 13 Create a Communications Plan for Core Team 14 Create a Communications Plan for Participants and Volunteers 15 Program Execution 16 Program Retrospective 17 Creating an Alumni Network

Start with alumni

After each cohort, integrate alumni into as many volunteer positions as possible. They are already familiar with the program and offer invaluable guidance to current cohort members.

docs.title: Step 1 — Review Program Resources and Create Program Templates
docs.text:
Step 1 of 17

Action
  • To align the program with company goals such as brand recognition, review all program documentation to gain a comprehensive understanding of the program.
  • Copy the program's templates to help guide you in the creation of your own program resources.
Guidance
  • Review of these documents helps clarify how the program operates, its intended outcomes, and how it contributes to broader company objectives.
  • Review of documents should be done prior to moving to Step 2.
  • Engage with whichever team runs the company's intern program.
Considerations
  • Will you utilize existing resources or develop new ones?
  • Since this program is heavily dependent on employee volunteers, does your company provide its employees with the freedom to take on initiatives outside of their daily work responsibilities?

Next: Step 2 — Engage Leadership :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Step 2 — Engage your Leadership Team
docs.text:
Step 2 of 17

Action

Obtain Leadership Team approval for program support and advocacy.

Guidance
  • Leadership Team approval is helpful in acquiring internship headcount, budget, and volunteer resources.
  • Start stakeholder discussions early — they are time-consuming.
  • Schedule extra time to prepare tailored stakeholder proposals and presentations.
  • Include the Recruiting Team in the Leadership Team for internship opportunity headcount/placement alignment.
  • Prepare a proposal that includes:
    • A storyline of why this program is important
    • Any metrics that help support your proposal
    • The overall timeline of the program
    • Clear program needs such as:
      • The involvement expected from leadership
      • An estimated budget during your initial conversation with leadership (refer to the budget section for guidance)
      • An estimated Program Team headcount
Considerations
  • Did you ensure time for leadership discussions before deadlines?
  • Did you customize presentations for each stakeholder for maximum buy-in?
  • Do you have support and advocacy during stakeholder meetings?

:material-arrow-left: Step 1 Step 3 :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Step 3 — Create Program Timeline and Set Key Milestones
docs.text:
Step 3 of 17

Action

Outline the main phases of the program's timeline and identify significant milestones.

Guidance

Use the program timeline example to build a proposal.

Considerations
  • What key dates do you need to set before engaging key stakeholders?

:material-arrow-left: Step 2 Step 4 :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Step 4 — Confirm Core Program Team
docs.text:
Step 4 of 17

Action

Define your internal team's structure based on the Core Team roles and how many students your cohort will support.

Guidance
  • Carefully manage any role changes to ensure all responsibilities are covered for seamless operation.
  • Suggested Core Program Team roles:
Role Responsibility Regional Program Lead Oversees program logistics, budget, communications, and speaker arrangements. Technical Lead Oversees the program's technical aspects. Requires coding knowledge and comfort with technical presentations. Mentors and Volunteers Lead Oversees volunteer coordination from start to finish. Recruiting Support Manages program launch marketing and supports interview and offer processes. Workshop MC (Optional) Leads workshops and keeps participants focused and engaged. MC role can be combined with the Regional Program Lead if additional headcount is not available.

Use alumni as MCs

Once you have program graduates, they make ideal MCs — they're familiar with the content and purpose of the program.

Considerations
  • Is there enough internal bandwidth for dedicated roles?
  • Does the cohort size demand dedicated roles?
  • Will roles be part-time or full-time positions?
  • Can the program be run by multiple teams, or does it require single-team alignment?

:material-arrow-left: Step 3 Step 5 :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Step 5 — Confirm if your Program is Virtual or In-Person
docs.text:
Step 5 of 17

Action

Choose virtual, in-person, or a hybrid program format, aligning with your company's expected working model.

Guidance

=== "Virtual" - For inaugural cohorts, virtual programs may be easier to execute. - Virtual formats allow you to engage a broader range of students and volunteers across different time zones, expanding the program's reach and a student's network. - Consider virtual programs for their cost-efficiency, especially if budget is a concern for inaugural cohorts.

=== "In-Person" - In-person benefits include targeting regional/specific schools, a pool of local participants, and genuine engagement and connections. - In-person programs may incur higher costs due to expenses such as meals, snacks, room rentals, workshop supplies, in-person volunteer requirements, and commuting stipends. - In-person programs may be more logistically difficult to plan.

Considerations
  • Can you afford the budget, space, and personnel for in-person?
  • Is the office accessible for students and volunteers during workshops?
  • Will in-person volunteer needs be met?
  • Does your team have the bandwidth to cover in-person logistics and overhead?

:material-arrow-left: Step 4 Step 6 :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Step 6 — Confirm Length of the Program
docs.text:
Step 6 of 17

Action

Space your workshops at least 7 weeks apart to allow time for assignments, grading, interview feedback, and office hours.

Guidance
  • The program should end with sufficient time for interviews and offers before internships begin, so that fellows can participate in the internship selection process.
  • Confirm your company's requirements and qualifications for interns.
  • Holidays can disrupt the cohort schedule due to time off for students and volunteers.
  • Keep in mind annual planning dates and other key events in your company's calendar that may impact volunteer availability.
Considerations
  • What are the internship start dates?
  • How many yearly internship cycles are there?
  • Can graduates of the program (alumni) be placed in any available internship cycle?
  • Do cohort dates align with multiple internship cycles?
  • Will the cohort schedule overlap with holidays?
  • What is the estimated length of assignments, and what's the reasonable completion time?
  • How often should mentor–fellow meetings be held?

:material-arrow-left: Step 5 Step 7 :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Step 7 — Confirm Size of your Cohort
docs.text:
Step 7 of 17

Action

Determine the size of your cohort.

Guidance
  • Confirm the anticipated number of interns to be hired in the upcoming cycle with the Recruiting Team.
  • To effectively test the curriculum and maximize ROI, consider starting with a moderate-sized initial cohort. This allows for validation of the curriculum's success before scaling to a larger number of students.
  • Begin with a cohort of at least 8–10 students for these reasons:
    • To account for potential absences and maintain engagement in breakout sessions.
    • Smaller cohorts may create undue pressure on students and not fully utilize volunteer time.
    • This size allows for easy pairing of students for activities.
    • Larger cohorts could overwhelm the Core Program Team during initial implementation.
Considerations
  • What percentage of internship opportunities would this program require if all students pass the internship interviews?
  • Should the cohort number be adjusted up or down based on that percentage?
  • Are there similar programs for potential marketing or process collaboration?
  • Will there be adequate volunteer support for the entire cohort?

:material-arrow-left: Step 6 Step 8 :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Step 8 — Confirm the Dates/Times of your Workshops
docs.text:
Step 8 of 17

Action

Collaborate with your Core Program Team to schedule optimal dates and times for your workshops.

Guidance
  • Full-day workshops are not recommended — they require extended breaks (including lunch) and can lead to exhaustion for the Core Program Team and students.
  • Target 1st/2nd-year students for optimal internship and full-time opportunity pipelines; align academic years/selection with program duration and hiring needs.
  • For maximum impact, programs should be completed with enough time to teach the curriculum at a reasonable pace, as it only supplements current coursework.
  • The cohort must end before internships start, allowing time for interviews, offers, acceptances, and relocation.
  • The program's essential milestones and timeline are created by planning backward from the internship start date.
  • Having multiple internship cycles will improve placement chances based on internship opportunities and business needs.
  • Avoid scheduling workshops during exam weeks, as this impacts assignments and mock interview prep. Reference academic school calendars when finalizing dates.
Considerations
  • Should workshops be full-day or half-day?
  • Will the cohort span one or two academic years?
  • What are your company's internship start and end dates?
  • How many annual internship cycles are offered?
  • Do program dates align with recruiting deadlines?
  • Are there any company-specific scheduling constraints to consider?
  • How will company holidays/events affect volunteer participation?
  • Do regional holidays/cultural norms need consideration?
  • What are university exam periods and holiday schedules?

:material-arrow-left: Step 7 Step 9 :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Step 9 — Confirm Program Budget
docs.text:
Step 9 of 17

Action

Refine cost areas; review and manage a budget tracker.

Guidance

=== "Virtual Program Costs" - SWAG for volunteers and student participants - Virtual engagement activities - Meal stipends/vouchers

=== "In-Person Program Costs" - SWAG for volunteers and student participants - In-person engagement activities - Catering - Supplies - Meeting/presentation space (if not hosted at the company's office) - Transportation costs (optional)

  • Think through your company's financial management practices and identify any concerns or questions.
  • At a minimum, include SWAG for volunteers to show appreciation and for students to celebrate their participation and reinforce branding.
Considerations
  • Is the program budget in alignment with other similar company program budgets?
  • Who is the responsible budget stakeholder?
  • Will program charges be required for the budget sponsor?

:material-arrow-left: Step 8 Step 10 :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Step 10 — Align Recruiting Strategy & Confirm Eligibility Requirements
docs.text:
Step 10 of 17

Action

Collaborate with the Recruiting Team and stakeholders to set the program's eligibility requirements based on your company's university recruiting strategy.

Guidance
  • Clearly define the purpose of this program and how it ties into university recruitment strategy.
  • Work with your Recruiting Team to enhance their current university recruiting strategy instead of reinventing the wheel.
  • Ensure eligibility criteria complies with regional laws and regulations for university hiring.
  • Employ "knockout" questions based on eligibility criteria to help filter applicants (e.g., graduation date, graduation month, required courses, experience level).
  • Provide clear and unambiguous definitions for eligibility criteria in the application.
  • Specify any disqualifying factors, such as AI usage or submission formatting errors.
Considerations

Demographics

  • Is it legally permissible to collect this demographic data within the application? Note that in many countries, legally protected characteristics such as race and sex should not constitute eligibility criteria or influence participant selection.
  • Whether demographic information should be tracked and analyzed, and if so, when and how?
  • What kind of demographic information should be tracked (e.g., first-generation college student, whether qualified for financial aid, whether worked during the school year)?

Concentration/Major

  • Which specific roles is the company recruiting for?
  • Are the names of majors or concentrations consistent across target universities?

Graduation Month/Year

  • What is the required graduation date (exact month/year) for fellows to be eligible for internships post-program?
  • How many annual internship cycles does your company offer, and can students apply to all of them?
  • Are there any post-internship enrollment obligations for participating students?

Location

  • What are the specific business requirements for the office(s) with open internship positions?
  • Which office location(s) currently have available internship headcount?
  • Is commuting to the office required for workshop attendance and/or internship participation?

General Eligibility

  • Is concurrent enrollment during internships permitted?
  • Are relocation benefits available for interns who reside beyond commuting range?
  • Does your company hire international students with existing visas/permits, and/or provide visa/work permit sponsorship?
  • Are students from non-traditional educational backgrounds (e.g., non-4-year institutions or coding bootcamps) eligible?
  • What are your company's legal guidelines regarding student hiring?

Legal Compliance

  • Ensure program compliance with laws and company policies covering data and hiring practices.

:material-arrow-left: Step 9 Step 11 :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Step 11 — Create your Program Curriculum
docs.text:
Step 11 of 17

Action

Develop the program curriculum to align with your company's success metrics.

Guidance

Workshop Structure

  • Schedule interactive activities for post-lunch sessions to maintain engagement; prioritize technical and complex sessions for the morning.
  • Incorporate interactive activities, including breakout sessions, throughout the program to balance lectures and reduce the need for frequent breaks.
  • Incorporate both technical and professional skills training to create a well-rounded curriculum.
  • Organize workshops around specific themes to enhance session cohesion and minimize topic shifts.
  • Curriculum should complement — not replace — school content.
  • Curriculum should teach fellows how to apply learnings to interviews and internships.
  • Consult leadership on relevant industry tools, themes, and practices for internship prep session topics.
  • Incorporate workshop feedback and questions promptly.
  • Workshop sessions should be designed so lessons are applicable to future workshops, assignments, and practices.

Mock Interview Question Bank

  • Questions should match the company's baseline for internship question difficulty.
  • Questions should align with technical practice assignment themes and build in difficulty over time.
  • There should be a handful of questions to choose from for each workshop in case fellows are able to solve more than one during the provided time.

Technical Practice Assignments

  • Themes should align with mock interview questions for practice and familiarization before the interview.
  • Technical practice assignments build on each other, starting with easier themes as the foundation.
Considerations
  • Will the curriculum target single or multiple graduation years and still remain relevant to all?
  • How many total instruction hours are planned, and can they be evenly distributed across all workshops?
  • Will the curriculum include specific engagement events?
  • What key technical or behavioral competencies should fellows develop?
  • Is there sufficient technical preparation and practice for student success?
  • Will sessions be lecture-based, interactive, or include breakouts?
  • Does the program offer enough session variety to maintain engagement?
  • Does the curriculum address relevant industry trends and student challenges?

:material-arrow-left: Step 10 Step 12 :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Step 12 — Create Volunteer Plan
docs.text:
Step 12 of 17

Action

Determine volunteer needs, target audience, and engagement strategies.

Guidance
  • Target at least 1:1 technical volunteer to cohort size for:
    • Entrance, internship, and mock interviews
    • 1:1 mentorship
  • Target 1:1 behavioral volunteer to cohort size for entrance interviews.
  • Recruit a larger volunteer pool to allow for replacements.
  • Engage early-career volunteers to build network and culture.
  • Avoid over-using the same volunteers.
  • Ensure all volunteer recruits are eligible.
  • Ensure all volunteers understand their roles and responsibilities.
  • Newer volunteers may not be ideal for complex mentorship.
  • Train interview volunteers to match company standards.
  • Show appreciation to volunteers based on your company's recognition platforms (e.g., all-hands shout-outs, company newsletters, SWAG, performance and promotion outcomes).
Considerations
  • Can volunteers hold multiple roles?
  • Are specific background requirements needed for roles?
  • What are the volunteers' time zones?

:material-arrow-left: Step 11 Step 13 :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Step 13 — Create a Communications Plan for Core Team
docs.text:
Step 13 of 17

Action

Establish a communications plan to:

  1. Align stakeholders and Core Team on key milestones and deadlines
  2. Understand timing of communication to participants and volunteers
Guidance
  • Provide consistent status updates to stakeholders.
  • Coordinate with other program communication plans.
  • Consider internal communication norms and practices within your company.
  • Keep communications high-level with metrics; avoid logistical information unless asked for.
  • Allow time for follow-ups.
  • Keep key info in the email body — minimize the need to click on links.
  • Use catchy subject lines.
  • Add a "TL;DR" summary at the top.
  • Be direct while storytelling; avoid being overly transactional.
Considerations
  • Who should send the communication? The Regional Program Lead should send initial communications to leadership and key stakeholders to establish a clear point of contact.
  • Personal or alias email? Sending from a personal email creates accountability and awareness.
  • Who should be CC'd or BCC'd for advocacy and visibility?
  • What communication channel has been most effective for your team (email, Slack, etc.)?

:material-arrow-left: Step 12 Step 14 :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Step 14 — Create a Communications Plan for Participants and Volunteers
docs.text:
Step 14 of 17

Action

Establish a communications plan in alignment with workshop dates.

Guidance
  • Coordinate with other program communication plans to avoid overlapping messages and asks to the same audience.
  • Consider internal communication norms and practices within your company.
  • Clearly state "ask" due dates.
  • Allow time for follow-ups.
  • Keep key info in the email body — minimize the need to click on links.
  • Use catchy subject lines.
  • Add a "TL;DR" summary at the top.
  • Be direct while storytelling; avoid being overly transactional.
  • Include the benefits of participation in the program as a volunteer.
Considerations
  • Who should send the communication?
    • Leadership should send initial volunteer communications to demonstrate support for their time and effort.
    • The Core Program Team can send any follow-up emails as needed.
  • Personal or alias email? Sending from an alias enables team alignment and cross-functional support as needed.
  • Where should responses be directed? Responses should be directed to an alias to ensure team alignment and cross-functional support.
  • Who should be CC'd or BCC'd?
  • What communication channel has been most effective for your team (email, Slack, etc.)?

:material-arrow-left: Step 13 Step 15 :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Step 15 — Program Execution
docs.text:
Step 15 of 17

Action

Put the plan into action: Launch the program!

Guidance

Refer to the detailed Program Execution Overview for the three-phase execution framework covering fellow selection, workshops, and internship outcomes.

:material-arrow-left: Step 14 Step 16 :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Step 16 — Program Retrospective
docs.text:
Step 16 of 17

Action

Create a program retrospective and share with key stakeholders.

Guidance
  • Ensure all feedback is summarized into an easily digestible format.
  • Include actual program spend against the approved budget.
  • Host retrospective syncs with the Core Program Team and key volunteers to encourage open discussion and feedback.
  • Include a summary of positives / negatives / action items.
  • Differentiate actionable feedback from subjective opinions.
Considerations
  • How can feedback best narrate your program's impact?

:material-arrow-left: Step 15 Step 17 :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Step 17 — Creating an Alumni Network
docs.text:
Step 17 of 17

Action

Cultivate a strong alumni network.

Guidance

Integrate alumni into as many aspects of your program as possible. They are familiar with the program and offer invaluable technical guidance, best practices, and relevant advice — significantly aiding current cohort members in overcoming challenges like imposter syndrome.

Considerations
  • Does your company allow external guest speakers if your alumni no longer work at your company?

You've completed the planning phase!

With all 17 steps addressed, you're ready to move into program execution. Head to the Program Execution section for the three-phase framework.

:material-arrow-left: Step 16 Program Execution :material-arrow-right:

docs.title: Roles & Responsibilities
docs.text: Successful execution of a Career Prep program depends on a well-defined team structure. This section outlines every role — both on the Core Program Team and in the broader volunteer pool.

docs.title: Core Program Team
docs.text:
While each role is vital to program execution, they may not require full-time staff. Percentage time is calculated based on a 35-hour week or 8-month cohort.

Role Time Commitment Key Focus Regional Program Lead ~700 hrs (~50% over 8 months) Program logistics, stakeholders, budget Recruiting Team ~436 hrs (~30% over 8 months) Marketing, interviews, offers Workshop MC ~40 hrs (~1% over 8 months) Workshop facilitation Technical Lead ~48 hrs (~3% over 8 months) Technical curriculum, interviews Mentor & Volunteer Lead ~116 hrs (~8% over 8 months) Mentor sourcing, coordination

docs.text: Role Time per Engagement Duration Mentors ~2 hrs/week Full cohort (8 months) Session Leads Up to 60 min/session Per workshop Mock Interviewers 70 min/interview Per workshop Technical Interviewers 70 min/interview Entrance & internship interviews Behavioral Interviewers 35 min/interview Entrance & internship interviews Application Reviewers ~4 min/application Application period

docs.title: Core Program Team
docs.text: While each role is vital to program execution, they may not require full-time staff. Detailed role descriptions and time commitments are available in the linked resources. Percentage time is calculated based on a 35-hour week or 8-month cohort.

docs.title: Regional Program Lead
docs.text:
Time commitment: ~700 hours (~50% time) over 8-month cohort

The Regional Program Lead is the central coordinator of the entire program.

Responsibilities:

  • Manages program logistics, timeline, stakeholders, and budget
  • Liaises between team and stakeholders
  • Oversees Core Team execution
  • Manages program timeline and milestones
  • Authors/oversees program communications
  • Confirms and creates workshop topics/agendas
  • Identifies workshop speakers
  • Reviews/implements workshop feedback

docs.title: Recruiting Team
docs.text:
Time commitment: ~436 hours (~30% time) over 8-month cohort

Responsibilities:

  • Confirms/finalizes regional internship headcount with the Recruiting Team and organizations
  • Creates marketing materials and leads application marketing/tracking
  • Secures technical/behavioral interviewers for all interviews
  • Schedules/reschedules all interviews
  • Sources applicants via university partnerships and target schools
  • Point of contact for recruiting questions on program Slack channels
  • Follows up with fellows during interviews and extends offers
  • Tracks competitor offers for metrics and industry insights
  • Tracks company offers post-cohort and updates cohort graduate (alumni) tracker

docs.title: Workshop MC
docs.text:
Time commitment: ~40 hours (~1% time) during 8-month cohort

The Workshop MC is the main company representative at each workshop. This role can be combined with the Regional Program Lead if additional headcount is not available. Program alumni make ideal MCs.

Responsibilities:

  • Main company representative at each workshop
  • Manages speaker slides
  • Creates workshop playlists
  • Keeps sessions on time and fellows engaged
  • Triages workshop questions

docs.title: Technical Lead
docs.text:
Time commitment: ~48 hours (~3% time) during 8-month cohort

Responsibilities:

  • Manages technical portion of cohort acceptance interview process:
    • Questions bank
    • Volunteer interview training
    • Score cards/evaluation
    • Reviews scores, makes recommendations/decisions
  • Manages mock interview question bank and score cards
  • Manages internship interview question bank and score cards
  • Authors/hosts technical training for volunteers
  • Authors/hosts 75-min technical sessions for fellows during each workshop
  • Hosts 60-min office hours between workshops
  • Answers technical questions across all channels
  • Creates/maintains code sharing platform for assignments and access

docs.title: Mentor & Volunteer Lead
docs.text:
Time commitment: ~116 hours (~8% time) over 8-month cohort

Responsibilities:

  • Sources/assigns technical mentors for the cohort
  • Liaises between Core Team, mentors, and fellows
  • Manages mock interview sourcing/scheduling for each workshop
  • Tracks mock interview/assignment submissions and follow-ups
  • Provides mentors with workshop recaps
  • Co-hosts office hours with Technical Lead
  • Point of contact for mentor/volunteer questions on Slack

docs.title: Volunteer Roles
docs.text: Volunteers are essential for program execution, fulfilling various roles. The number of volunteers needed depends on their backgrounds, availability, and capacity.

docs.title: Mentors
docs.text:
Time commitment ~2 hours/week Duration Entire cohort (8 months) Eligibility Technical background required (must know how to code)

Responsibilities:

  • Conducts at least two 30-min meetings with their fellow between workshops
  • Attends mentor onboarding and reviews training materials before cohort launch
  • Grades fellow's technical practice assignments
  • Reviews assignments and mock interview feedback with their fellow
  • Updates mentee/mentor data in the mentor tracker for accountability
  • Submits mid-year and year-end program feedback surveys

docs.title: Session Leads
docs.text:
Time commitment Up to 60 min/session Duration Per workshop Eligibility Technical or non-technical background, depending on the workshop theme

Responsibilities:

  • Participates in a 30-minute prep sync to align workshop expectations
  • Develops/updates slides and contributes them to the main workshop deck
  • Confirms which speakers will handle screen sharing
  • Conducts a dry-run if necessary

docs.title: Mock Interviewers
docs.text:
Time commitment 70 minutes/interview (60 min interview + 10 min for feedback submission) Duration Per workshop Eligibility Technical background required (must know how to code)

Responsibilities:

  • Reviews mock interviewer training materials and question bank
  • Reviews the fellow's resume before the interview
  • Conducts the mock interview using the company's preferred platform
  • Provides live feedback in the last 10 minutes, if time allows
  • Submits feedback immediately post-interview

docs.title: Technical Interviewers
docs.text:
Conduct interviews to assess candidate suitability for both cohort admission and potential internship placement.

Time commitment 70 minutes/interview (60 min interview + 10 min for feedback form submission) Duration Cohort entrance interviews and/or internship interviews Eligibility Technical background required (must know how to code); must have completed required company interview trainings

Responsibilities:

  • Reviews interviewer training documents and questions bank
  • Attends the program-specific interviewer training
  • Reviews the fellow's resume before the interview
  • Submits feedback immediately post-interview

docs.title: Behavioral Interviewers
docs.text:
Time commitment 35 minutes/interview (30 min interview + 5 min for feedback form submission) Duration Cohort entrance interviews and/or internship interviews Eligibility No specific background requirements; must have completed required company interview trainings

Responsibilities:

  • Reviews interviewer training documents and questions bank
  • Attends the program-specific interviewer training
  • Reviews the fellow's resume before the interview
  • Submits feedback immediately post-interview

docs.title: Cohort Application Reviewers
docs.text:
Time commitment ~4 minutes/application (total time determined by application-to-volunteer ratio) Duration Application review period Eligibility Technical background recommended

Responsibilities:

  • Attends application reviewer training
  • Adds applicant summaries and reviewer accept/reject recommendations to the applicant tracker
